newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RUGBY LEAGUE-AUSTRALIAN RIVALS TALK UNITY.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY LEAGUE-AUSTRALIAN RIVALS TALK UNITY.

text.p: Australia's warring rugby league competitions -- spurned by the fans and bleeding dollars by the bucketful -- could soon declare peace.

The Australian Rugby League (ARL), which controlled the game until media tycoon Rupert Murdoch set up his Super League this year in a fanfare of publicity, said on Wednesday it would work towards a single national premiership.
"It does appear...that there is the opportunity to at least investigate uniting the game again," ARL chief executive Neil Whittaker told a news conference.
However he warned that if talks did not progress quickly, the ARL would go ahead with its 12-team Optus Cup in 1998 in competition with the 10-team Super League.
For its part, Super League said it welcomed the news and looked forward to future discussions.
Rugby league, the main winter sport in New South Wales and Queensland states, has suffered financially and in the eyes of fans following a protracted legal battle to get Super League on to the field.
The new competition kicked off in February, the culmination of a long battle by Murdoch to poach the game away from the ARL and make it part of his sports-driven global pay-television network.
But gates have been disappointing -- the big winner appears to have been Australian rules football -- and both sides have conceded that rugby league can only support one premiership.
Whittaker and News Ltd director of sport Ian Frykberg have held early talks, only revealed in recent days, but unification still faces the sticking point of financial control.

Super League is reported to have offered a peace plan which would see it run an elite national competition, while the ARL would run a second tier competition, but also have control of national and junior football.

"We have invested hundreds of millions of dollars into the game and the idea is that the clubs should evenutally become profitable," Frykberg told the Sydney Morning Herald. "We don't want to walk away from that."
However, the ARL, which has run the game in Australia for 90 years, wants to continue to adminster all tiers of the game.
"Our position hasn't changed...the right thing for the game is to have the national body which represents the game control the game at all levels," said Whittaker.
The negotiations will be complicated by the network of shifting loyalties among backers of the two groups.
The ARL has the support of communications group Optus, which is paying each of its 12 teams A$1.8 million (US$1.35 million) in 1997, and shows the ARL on its pay-TV station.

Murdoch's Foxtel pay-TV has Super League, while Australia's richest man Kerry Packer, a one-time staunch ARL backer, struck a deal with Murdoch in January and now has terrestrial broadcast rights for both leagues.
Whittaker said Optus had agreed to back a separate 1998 competition if necessary, and acknowledged the impact pay television was having on rugby league.
"This game is going to need significant support from all pay-TV companies into the future to get us back on a community-owned, financially-sustainable footing," he said.
